tagline: Marble capital beside a burning crater
overview:
Turkmenistan lies in Central Asia on the eastern shore of the Caspian Sea, bordering Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Afghanistan and Iran. The Karakum, a sandy desert, covers around 70 percent of the country's 488,000 km², an area a little larger than Sweden.

About 6 million people live here, mostly in oases along the desert edges. Turkmen is the state language and Russian is also widely spoken. Ashgabat, the capital, was rebuilt after a catastrophic earthquake and is now a city of white marble buildings, gold domes and enormous monuments; it holds a world record for the highest density of white marble-clad buildings.

Turkmenistan is a presidential republic and one of the most closed countries in the world, with tightly controlled media and few visitors. It holds some of the largest natural gas reserves on Earth, which fund government spending and, for many years, provided households with free gas, water and electricity.
landAndNature: The Karakum, meaning black sand, spreads across most of the country in long dune ridges and gravel plains where summer temperatures can exceed 45°C. At Darvaza a gas crater has been burning since it was set alight decades ago, a fiery pit in the desert that locals call the Door to Hell. The Kopet Dag mountains rise along the Iranian border, and the Amu Darya river waters the east. The Karakum Canal, one of the longest irrigation canals in the world, carries river water hundreds of kilometers to cotton fields, and that diversion of water is one reason the Aral Sea to the north has shrunk drastically. Akhal-Teke horses, famous for their metallic golden sheen and endurance, are a national treasure, and goitered gazelles and wild ass roam reserves.
peopleAndCulture: Turkmen identity rests on tribes, horses and carpets. Hand-knotted Turkmen rugs in deep red with repeating octagon motifs called guls are so central that the guls appear on the national flag, and there is a public holiday devoted to carpets. The Akhal-Teke horse, bred here for thousands of years, has its own festival too. Traditional dress includes bright embroidered dresses and tall sheepskin hats. Bread baked in a clay tandyr oven is treated with great respect, and plov, green tea and fermented camel milk called chal are everyday foods. The dutar, a two-stringed lute, accompanies bagshy singers who recite long epic poems. Most Turkmen are Muslim, and family celebrations are large and formal.
history: The oasis city of Merv on the Silk Road was, by some estimates, the largest city in the world around 1150, a center of learning with great libraries, until Mongol armies destroyed it in 1221 and killed much of its population. Nisa, near Ashgabat, was a capital of the Parthian empire 2,000 years ago. Turkmen tribes herded and traded across the deserts for centuries. The Russian empire conquered the region in the 1880s after heavy fighting at Geok Tepe. Under Soviet rule from the 1920s, nomads were forced to settle, cotton growing was expanded with massive irrigation, and religion was suppressed. An earthquake destroyed Ashgabat in 1948, killing tens of thousands. Turkmenistan became independent in 1991, and its first president, Saparmurat Niyazov, ruled with a strong personality cult until his death in 2006.
funFacts: The Darvaza gas crater in the Karakum desert has burned continuously for decades and glows orange at night.
Ashgabat holds a Guinness record for the world's highest concentration of white marble-covered buildings.
Turkmenistan's flag is the most detailed national flag in the world, showing five carpet designs down one side.
The Akhal-Teke horse has a coat that can shine like polished metal, and one appears on the country's coat of arms.
Ancient Merv was possibly the largest city on Earth in the 1100s, before the Mongols destroyed it.
